FSAE front wing and nose cone

CCNY FSAE Aero division and ME 473 Senior Design 1, Spring 2026
215 NDownforce at 14 m/s, most conservative result (target: over 180 N)
3Wing elements: one E423 main element and two S1223 flaps
355 mmMain element chord, at a -5 degree angle of attack
10Spacing and angle setups tested for the second element

What the wing is for

The club's Formula SAE car is open-wheel, so the front tires sit right behind the wing. A front wing makes downforce, but designing only for downforce isn't enough. The air leaving the wing hits the tires, so wake management matters just as much. The goal was a wing that makes downforce while managing its wake so that it clears the front tires.

Team: Derek Chen, Rin Curzio, Gerasimos Patsili, Soterios Homenides, Sandra Lu, and Oliver Wolak. Advisor: Prof. Richard La Grotta.

Requirements

  • Over 180 N of downforce at 14 m/s (50 km/h), checked with CFD
  • At least two elements, with airflow directed up and outward away from the front tires
  • Wing under 20 lb and nose cone under 4 lb (not counting the impact attenuator)
  • No contact with the wheels, hubs, or suspension, and it must follow the 2026 FSAE rules
  • Buildable by the team with a CNC, wire cutter, and carbon fiber with epoxy

Choosing the airfoils

The car runs at low Reynolds numbers, so I started with 2D simulations in ANSYS Fluent on a range of single airfoils at -5 degrees. Fluent runs a 1 m span with symmetry at the ends, so there are no wingtip losses. High-camber profiles with a steep drop in thickness behind the thickest point did best. The Eppler 423 had the best lift-to-drag ratio, so it became the main element at a 355 mm chord.

AirfoilDownforce (N per m of span)Lift-to-drag ratio
E423110.881.5
CH10114.379.7
GOE 448106.379.2
E420115.868.4
S1223111.966.9

Preliminary 2D results with the k-omega model, 305 mm chord, -5 degrees. Five of the 13 airfoils tested.

An early "M loft" main element, with a bowed trailing edge to bend the wake away from the tires, didn't add downforce. It was also harder to mesh and to manufacture, so we dropped it.

Adding a second element

Once the wing was sized for the real car, the flow from a single element didn't clear the wheels. The second element was laid out like the flaps of an airliner set for landing, passing the flow from one foil to the next. The S1223 sent the wake a couple of degrees higher than the E423 would, so it became the second element at a 200 mm chord and -15 degrees. It adds up to 30 N of downforce per meter of span in the worst-case turbulence setup.

I compared ten spacing and angle setups. High-speed air under the second element shouldn't disturb the slower air above the main element, and too much overlap takes downforce away from the main element. Some overlap was kept so the whole wing stays short, which keeps its mounting position adjustable on the car.

Adding a third element

The suspension team's track width estimate capped the wing at 1,372 mm wide and the nose cone at 312 mm. With that geometry and a 7.5 x 16 inch tire, two elements still left the wake short of the top of the tire. The third element is a pure flap whose only job is to redirect the wake.

An S1223 at a 100 mm chord and -30 degrees left the wake about 2 inches short. At -45 degrees the wake cleared the tire, with no loss of downforce.

Making the simulation realistic

With help from Mike Wegrzyniak, who specializes in internal-flow CFD, we improved the 3D model:

  • Set minimum feature size and curvature to 1 mm so sharp edges mesh properly
  • Added a body of influence around the foils, so the mesh is fine only where it matters
  • Modeled wheel spin with a moving wall rotating at 69 rad/s about the tire's centroid
  • Ran half the car with a symmetry boundary once the nose cone, monocoque, wing, and tires were all in the model

The final runs used the k-omega SST model at a 14 m/s inlet speed. The most complex mesh gave the most conservative result of 215 N of downforce, with turbulence and the spinning tire included.

Nose cone

The nose cone's main job is to house the impact attenuator, the crumple zone of the car. Its aerodynamic effect is limited, but it can add some downforce to support the wing. After the early version was flagged for a redesign, it was reshaped with a downward curve, and it has to stay compatible with the attenuator and the monocoque.

Pathlines taken from the center of the car.

Manufacturing and testing plans

A sponsor is expected to supply scrap carbon fiber. The plan is to form 2 to 4 layers of carbon fiber and epoxy over foam cut with a hot wire and wood templates, with an internal spar or rib cut by water jet, CNC, or laser, attached to a plywood or aluminum base. Stress simulations would predict where the greatest deflection will be.

Testing would cover weight, deflection, and, if possible, a wind tunnel run to see whether the physical wing matches the CFD. Downforce is the main number to check.

FEA Bike project

ME 371, City College of New York, Fall 2025
6Parts analyzed: frame, fork, wheel, handlebars, sprocket, and crank with pedal
1.6Frame factor of safety under a 1,275 N load at the seat
13Fork buckling factor of safety
6.39Sprocket factor of safety under 1,000 N on two teeth

The project

I modeled a custom 29 inch BMX bike in SolidWorks, based on the SE Bikes 29 inch BMX, and used finite element analysis (FEA) to check whether its geometry and material make a viable design. My version changes the frame geometry, adds more durable forks, and gives a slightly more upright riding position by shortening the frame and giving the fork a steeper angle, so the front wheel pivot stays in the same place.

The most important feature is a custom 5-spoke wheel meant to prevent bent spokes, a common failure on BMX bikes. A tall 1 cm lip around the rim keeps the wheel strong with less material, and each spoke is trimmed to an I-beam cross section to save weight and keep strength.

Instructors: Dr. Peyman Honarmandi and Dr. Yesim Kokner.

How it was tested

Every part was analyzed in SolidWorks Simulation, and I cross-checked the frame with my own FEA code in MATLAB. The loads were deliberately extreme: 1,000 N is roughly 225 lb, the full body weight of a heavy rider, applied to a single part.

PartLoad (N)Where appliedPeak stress (MPa)Factor of safety
Frame1,275Seat tube, where a bottomed-out seat contacts the frame1721.6
Fork1,275Normal to the fork1401.96 static, 13 buckling
Crank arm and pedal1,000Pedal face2091.31
Sprocket1,000Shared by two teeth436.39
Handlebars750Split between the bar ends2731.01
Wheel (no tire)1 m dropImpact on the rim2661.6

Yield strength used: 275 MPa.

Frame

I applied 1,275 N at the seat tube, where a fully bottomed-out seat would contact the frame, with a roller at the fork mount and a hinge at the rear wheel. The frame needed a curvature-based mesh to be analyzed at all.

For the hand check, I reduced the frame to a 2D model with seven members. The two rear stays were combined into one member with their combined cross-section area, and the fork pair got the same treatment. I then wrote a frame-element FEA code in MATLAB with 1,275 N vertical loads at the seat and stem. The largest axial member force was about 1,190 N in a tube of about 180 mm², so member stresses stayed very low. That points to stress concentrations at the joints as the source of the higher peak stress in the 3D model.

Fork

The fork carries a high axial load, so it can fail by buckling, the same thing that bows a metal ruler pressed into a table, at a much lower load than it takes to yield it. I ran a buckling study with fixed-fixed conditions, because there is no axle to keep the two legs from deflecting apart. With 1,275 N applied, the buckling factor of safety was 13. A fixed-fixed beam carries about double a fixed-free one, so even the more conservative case stays above 6.

A buckling study ignores stress concentrations, so I also ran a static study. It gave a factor of safety of 1.6 and showed stress concentrating where the fork splits.

Wheel

The wheel was designed to survive repeated impacts, so I tested it with a drop test. A 1 m drop showed that the main point of failure is the spoke-to-rim connection, although the wheel still maintains a factor of safety of 1.6. A 5 m drop gave a stress of 274.75 MPa, which is just at the failing point. Both tests were run without a tire, which would greatly improve impact performance, since a tire absorbs a lot of energy and acts like a spring, returning some of that energy to the ground.

Handlebars

I loaded the bars with 375 N per side, spread over the 120 mm where the grips sit, which is like a 175 lb rider doing a dip. The stem was modeled with the bars, since the two transfer load together to the fork. The 73 cm width makes the bars prone to bending, and the peak stress reached 273 MPa, a factor of safety of 1.01. This is harsher than real riding: the load is perfectly vertical, while a rider's arms angle outward and reduce the vertical force.

Sprocket, crank, and pedal

The 4 mm thick sprocket, modeled with its crank screw hole, handled 1,000 N on just two teeth with a factor of safety of 6.39.

The crank and pedal were modeled together in the level position, with 1,000 N on the pedal and the arm fixed where it mounts to the crankshaft. With no drivetrain to share the load, this is a conservative test, and it gave a factor of safety of 1.31. The pedal bends unevenly because the model uses a solid connection in place of a spindle, which picks up moment at the far end that a real spindle and bottom bracket would relieve.

Takeaways

Parts that came close to yielding in early trials were improved with a larger standard tube size or adjusted geometry. Based on these simulations, the bike should handle riders over 200 lb. Titanium would add strength, but its cost makes it impractical. This is a prototype with room to improve.

245 Park Avenue: data and sound masking installation

Team lead
190Data drops
23Wireless access points
2Fiber-optic risers
300+Home runs terminated in the IDF

Project overview

From June to October, I led a team of up to four technicians on a data cabling and sound masking installation at 245 Park Avenue. The project used Leviton data infrastructure and LOGISON sound masking systems. The scope included 190 data drops, 23 wireless access points, and two fiber-optic risers, with more than 300 home runs terminated in the Intermediate Distribution Frame (IDF), the building's main network room.

Cable pathways and field installation

The first two weeks focused on preparing cable pathways throughout the floor. This involved installing cable hooks, navigating existing ductwork, maintaining at least 12 inches of separation from electrical home runs, and keeping all pathways clear of sprinkler systems. Once the pathways were ready, cables were pulled from their designated drop locations to the area outside the IDF, where they would later be organized and prepared for termination.

Completed sound masking panel and SM section print.

IDF buildout and support design

After completing the field cabling, I moved on to preparing the IDF. The first step was building the ladder rack, which supports the cables as they enter the cabinets and terminate at the patch panels connected to the network switches.

Because the ladder rack spanned 12.5 feet, additional structural support was needed beyond the standard 10-foot support spacing. To solve this, I developed what our team nicknamed the "biplane support." Using beam clamps to suspend Kindorf strut from a structural I-beam, I created a second support point for the ladder rack. This provided a secure mounting solution while working around the limited space and obstacles commonly found in crowded ceilings.

Freshly grouped wires with complete ladder rack.

Termination planning and quality control

One of the main challenges was that a termination schedule had not been provided. I took responsibility for creating one based on standard patterns from previous projects. This schedule allowed me to organize the cables into groups and assign them to the correct cabinets and patch panels before termination.

Each patch panel accommodated 48 cables, organized into groups of 12. After grouping and cutting the cables to length, I dressed them onto the ladder rack according to their designated cabinets. This kept the installation organized, made the final layout easier to follow, and helped simplify future troubleshooting and maintenance.

I completed the IDF terminations over the course of a week while my team handled the field-side terminations. Once all connections were completed, the cables were tested using a Fluke Networks cable tester. Any wiring errors or failed tests were addressed to ensure the installation met the required standards.

Terminated and dressed IDF.

Team leadership and jobsite safety

Safety and coordination were important throughout the project. Working with a team of technicians taught me the importance of staying aware of both my own surroundings and the people working around me. We completed pre-shift safety forms every morning and addressed hazards as they arose, including drilling debris, ladder work at elevation, sprinkler heads, and live electrical splice boxes above the ceiling.

Working on a union jobsite alongside an experienced superintendent from JT Magen also gave me valuable experience coordinating with other trades. Clear communication and cooperation helped us work through unexpected obstacles without compromising safety or installation quality. Throughout the project, I made it a priority to keep the team organized, resolve issues as they came up, and maintain progress toward the project deadline.

Project outcome

The installation was completed one week before the client's move-in date, with every cable accounted for and tested. This project gave me valuable hands-on experience in infrastructure installation, technical planning, team leadership, and field problem-solving. It also reinforced the importance of creating organized, maintainable systems and adapting engineering solutions to the practical constraints of an active construction site.
